source_text: Post paucos dies rumor cucurrit ut audiremur. Superuenit autem et de ciuitate pater meus, consumptus taedio, et ascendit ad me, ut me deiceret, dicens: Filia, miserere canis meis; miserere patri, si dignus sum a te pater uocari; si his te manibus ad hunc florem aetatis prouexi, si te praeposui omnibus fratribus tuis: ne me dederis in dedecus hominum. Aspice fratres tuos, aspice matrem tuam et materteram, aspice filium tuum, qui post te uiuere non poterit. Depone animos; ne uniuersos nos extermines: nemo enim nostrum libere loquetur, si tu aliquid fueris passa. Haec dicebat quasi pater pro sua pietate, basians mihi manus, et se ad pedes meos iactans et lacrimans me iam non filiam nominabat, sed dominam. Et ego dolebam casum patris mei, quod solus de passione mea gauisurus non esset de toto genere meo; et confortaui eum dicens: Hoc fiet in illa catasta quod deus uoluerit; scito enim nos non in nostra potestate esse futuros, sed in dei. Et recessit a me contristatus.
pass_a_gloss: After a few days a rumor ran that we were going to be given a hearing. And my father also came suddenly from the city, worn away by anguish, and came up to me in order to cast me down, saying: Daughter, have pity on my grey hairs; have pity on your father, if I am worthy to be called father by you; if with these hands I have brought you to this flower of age, if I have set you before all your brothers: do not give me over to the disgrace of men. Look at your brothers, look at your mother and your aunt, look at your son, who will not be able to live after you. Lay aside your resolve; do not destroy us all together: for none of us will speak freely, if you suffer anything. He kept saying this as a father out of his love, kissing my hands, and throwing himself at my feet and weeping he no longer called me daughter, but lady. And I grieved for the fall of my father, because he alone of all my kin would not be going to rejoice over my suffering; and I strengthened him saying: On that platform what God wills will happen; for know that we are not going to be in our own power, but in God's. And he went away from me grieved.
pass_b_english: A few days later word went round that our hearing was coming. Then my father arrived from the city, eaten up with grief, and climbed up to see me to break my resolve. He said, Daughter, pity my grey hairs. Pity your father, if I still deserve to be called father by you, if with these hands I raised you to this bloom of life, if I set you above all your brothers. Do not hand me over to public shame. Look at your brothers, look at your mother and your aunt, look at your child, who cannot live without you. Give up this resolve, or you will destroy us all. None of us will ever speak freely again if anything happens to you.

He said this as a father pleading from love, kissing my hands and casting himself at my feet, and through his tears he no longer called me daughter but lady. I grieved over my father's affliction, because he alone of all my kin would find no joy in my suffering. And I steadied him with these words: What God wills is what will happen on that scaffold. Know this: we shall not be in our own keeping, but in God's. Then he left me, heavy with sorrow.

lemmas.gloss: raised platform for trial or punishment

choices.why: ablative plural of canus, a conventional plea to a parent's old age rather than to dogs
deicio here is figurative pressure to make her fall from her stand, not physical throwing
catasta in a trial context is the raised platform where the accused stands, matching audiremur
